To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) outsourcing increases with the relative price of inputs and with the relative cost of customization; (ii) outsourcing increases with search costs in the domestic market and decreases with search costs in foreign markets; (iii) outsourcing increases with contract enforceability in domestic markets and with contract enforceability abroad; (iv) outsourcing increases with domestic market thickness and decreases with foreign market thickness.

(a) the degree of outsourcing is higher when the market for inputs is thin and (b) the degree of international outsourcing is higher when search is costly, the cost of customization is low, and when the contracting environment is more complete in the country where the final good is produced.

the determinants of outsourcing are similar in many ways to the determinants of trade in intermediate inputs.

the extent of international outsourcing is determined by the interplay of the market for input suppliers and the institutional environment in each country, as opposed to the relative factor endowments of the two countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
outsourcing is not necessarily more prevalent in countries with more flexible labor markets.
outsourcing is a two-edged sword.
